The speaker describes Microsoft as a 'violent ride' with zero returns until 2015/16, noting it was hard to hold over the period of the financial crisis and subsequent drops.
The speaker thinks Walmart is a business that does well but needs to be so good, and finds retail very hard and generally not interested.
The speaker views Costco as a 'cookie cutter' business with a well-defined model and appreciates its optionality, though notes it is richly priced.
The speaker notes that Starbucks started serving alcohol and has a higher-end coffee option, which changes the paradigm, but the market doesn't appreciate the uncertainty.
The speaker does not understand Amazon's retail business because the last mile delivery cost is so expensive, but it doesn't matter if he doesn't understand it.
The speaker notes that Nick Sleep's three-stock portfolio included Amazon, Costco, and Berkshire, and that he returned all the capital he was running.

thesis: This episode argues that successful investing often involves identifying 'cookie cutter' businesses with well-defined models and strong moats, even if they are richly priced, while avoiding complex retail businesses that are hard to understand. It highlights the importance of optionality and the ability to hold through periods of uncertainty, as seen in the speaker's experiences with companies like Costco, Amazon, and Berkshire Hathaway. The speaker also emphasizes the value of buybacks and the potential for significant returns in companies with intense capital allocation strategies.
